title: Adjectives and the construct chain

objectives.can: Match an adjective to its noun in gender, number and state, and read 'X of Y' in its three Aramaic forms.

explanation.summary: An Aramaic adjective follows its noun and agrees with it in gender, number and state. To say 'X of Y' Aramaic has three ways: two nouns joined as a construct chain, the little word דִּי between them, or a suffix on the first noun that points ahead to the second.

sections.heading: Adjectives agree with their noun
body: An attributive adjective, one that describes a noun directly, stands after the noun and matches it in three things: gender, number and state. In לְיַמָּא רַבָּא, 'to the great sea' (Daniel 7:2), the noun יַמָּא is masculine singular determined, and the adjective רַבָּא is masculine singular determined too. In חֵיוָן רַבְרְבָן, 'great beasts' (Daniel 7:3), noun and adjective are both feminine plural absolute.

The state is what is new for a reader of other languages. If the noun is determined, the adjective takes the determined ending as well; if the noun is absolute, so is the adjective. So בָּבֶל רַבְּתָא (Daniel 4:27) is 'Babylon the great': the adjective is feminine and determined like the city it describes.

sections.heading: When an adjective does not agree in state
body: An adjective that is the predicate of a clause, not an attribute, is usually in the absolute state, even when the noun it speaks of is determined. In Daniel 2:31 Daniel tells the king what he saw, and says of the image: צַלְמָא דִּכֵּן רַב, 'this image was mighty'. The noun צַלְמָא is determined; רַב is absolute, because it says what the image was. Compare מֶלֶךְ רַב in Daniel 2:10, where the same adjective sits after its noun in the absolute state and simply describes it.
So: right after a noun, the adjective matches its state; standing on its own as the thing said about a noun, it is usually absolute.

sections.heading: 'Of', first way: the construct chain
body: The simplest way to say 'X of Y' is to put the two nouns next to each other with the first in the construct state. The second noun is in whatever state the meaning needs. In רוּחֵי שְׁמַיָּא, 'the winds of heaven' (Daniel 7:2), רוּחֵי is the construct plural and שְׁמַיָּא the determined noun. In בֵּית אֱלָהָא, 'the house of God' (Ezra 5:2), בֵּית is the construct and אֱלָהָא the determined noun.

Only the first noun is in the construct state, and it normally has no other word between it and the noun that completes it. If the chain also has an adjective, the adjective stands after the whole chain and agrees with the last noun: in עֲבֵד אֱלָהָא חַיָּא, 'servant of the living God' (Daniel 6:21), חַיָּא is determined and matches אֱלָהָא, not עֲבֵד. In רוּחַ אֱלָהִין קַדִּישִׁין (Daniel 4:5), the plural absolute adjective matches אֱלָהִין.

sections.heading: 'Of', second way: דִּי between two nouns
body: The second way puts the little word דִּי between the nouns, and the first noun can then keep its ordinary form. Aramaic uses this way very often; grammarians note that it is common when the first noun is determined or when a plain chain would be hard to read. In Ezra 5:17 the two ways meet: בֵּית גִּנְזַיָּא דִּי מַלְכָּא is 'the house of the treasures of the king', where the first two nouns form a construct chain and דִּי links the whole chain to the king.
The same word דִּי also means 'who', 'which' and 'that'. The lesson on particles returns to it; for now note that between two nouns it is usually 'of'.

sections.heading: 'Of', third way: a suffix that looks ahead
body: The third way puts a pronominal suffix on the first noun and then names the owner with דִּי. It is like saying 'his name, of God'. In Daniel 2:20 the words שְׁמֵהּ דִּי אֱלָהָא are 'the name of God', literally 'his name, that of God'. In Ezra 5:11 עַבְדוֹהִי דִי אֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּא is 'the servants of the God of heaven', literally 'his servants, of the God of heaven'.
Notice that all three ways can combine, as in the last example, where a suffix, דִּי and a construct chain (אֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּא) stand together. The pronominal suffixes have a lesson of their own.

misunderstandings: The adjective does not come before the noun. In Aramaic it stands after it, and after the whole construct chain.
In a chain the adjective is not always with the nearer noun. Read the state: in עֲבֵד אֱלָהָא חַיָּא the adjective is determined, so it belongs to אֱלָהָא, because עֲבֵד is a construct.
דִּי is not always 'of'. It is also the relative word 'who' or 'which', and it can introduce clauses. Between two nouns it often means 'of', but check whether a verb or a new clause follows.

Not every form in a grammar's table occurs in these texts. The table above, which draws on the two adjectives רַב and רַבְרַב for 'great', has gaps where the Aramaic of the Bible has no example. Do not fill a gap from memory of another dialect.

deeper.heading: The same job in two ways
body: Grammarians note that the construct chain is the older and shorter way, and that the use of דִּי grows in later Aramaic, until in some dialects the chain is rare. In Daniel and Ezra both are alive, and the choice often seems to depend on how definite the first noun is and how long the second is. There is no simple rule that predicts every case.

examples.analysis: רוּחֵי שְׁמַיָּא is a construct chain: רוּחֵי is the construct plural and שְׁמַיָּא the determined noun that completes it. לְיַמָּא רַבָּא then shows adjective agreement: noun and adjective are both masculine singular determined. The English edition shows 'the four winds of the heaven' and 'the great sea'.
